title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes (model_calls_used = 301) and produced baseline = 299/300 valid configurations (99.667%) and guarded = 300/300 valid configurations (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered power calculation assumed a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 and targeted a 50% relative reduction in fail rate (≈+30 percentage points absolute); the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidates that planning assumption. We report preregistered design, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a short post‑hoc sensitivity statement grounded in archived contingency counts, and operational and methodological recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. Execution and analysis artifacts are archived with the run.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent into device configuration can accelerate network operations but creates operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Recent literature and architectural proposals increasingly recommend generate→verify→repair patterns that combine probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators or simulators to reduce misconfiguration risk. However, rigorous preregistered A/B experiments quantifying misconfiguration‑rate reductions for bounded guarded pipelines are scarce.

This work implements a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline: one shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), a frozen deterministic validator that performs rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, and at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. Our core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment (N=300) with deterministic seed generation and full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) an evidence‑grounded analysis showing that the observed near‑ceiling baseline undermined preregistered power assumptions; (3) operational and methodological recommendations (task difficulty calibration, paired sampling semantics, and repair budget design) for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Prior work establishes both promise and risk for LLM‑assisted NetOps. Surveys and system papers show that LLMs can synthesize configuration templates from intent but exhibit failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety. Cross‑domain studies in medical QA and code generation show that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; NetOps architectural proposals recommend deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets and generate→verify→repair pipelines for agentic workflows. Despite these convergent recommendations, we found few preregistered, paired A/B experiments that (a) use a deterministically generated task bank, (b) fix a frozen validator implementation, and (c) bound the automated repair budget for inference about first‑pass misconfiguration rate. Our study addresses that controlled gap and situates its findings relative to the closest operationally motivated proposals and empirical demonstrations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) prior to execution and the preregistration record is archived with the run; the preregistration planning assumptions (including the baseline pass rate = 0.40 used for power calculations) are recorded in the execution manifest. Confirmatory hypotheses were H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces the first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus plain single‑shot generation; and H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations.

Design and sampling: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds produced by the frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") was presented to both arms: baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same candidate validated and, if invalid, subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The execution contract fixed initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Using a shared initial candidate increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of informative discordant pairs compared to independent draws; this pairing semantics was preregistered and is material to power and inference.

Model, validator, and runtime: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. A frozen deterministic netops validator/repair adapter implemented rule‑ and dependency‑based checks (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and produced canonicalized ASTs, normalized configurations, and violation codes used for binary pass/fail scoring. Execution used the preregistered retry and missingness policies: one provider retry allowed per failed call and the primary analysis treatment 'complete_pair_primary' (drop pairs only if both calls failed). Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls (shared generation for each pair counted once, plus a single repair-stage model call in the guarded arm).

Primary estimand and analysis: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. We report absolute risk reduction with 95% confidence intervals, using a paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the absolute paired difference as prespecified. Secondary analyses (exploratory) include repair success rate with exact binomial (Clopper–Pearson) intervals and sensitivity analyses addressing missingness and contamination. All per‑task artifacts, validator traces, and repair traces were archived; details and artifact names are recorded in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and outcome summary: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, repair calls invoked = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; contamination checks flagged no deterministic exact duplicates among preregistered seeds; no exclusions or replacements were executed. Primary outcome counts (archive‑derived): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These counts are produced directly from the archived paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv artifacts.

Statistical inference: Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The absolute paired difference estimate (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 0.0033333333 (1/300). Paired bootstrap (percentile) 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729), as reported in the archived analysis artifacts. Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair call corrected the only initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1). The Clopper–Pearson exact 95% CI for a binomial numerator 1 of 1 is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting wide uncertainty given a single observed repair case.

Post‑hoc sensitivity quantification: The observed discordant pair count (n10 + n01 = 1) imposes a hard limit on resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 — the point estimate. Because McNemar's exact two‑sided test is driven by the pairwise discordants, an observed pattern of (1,0) (n10=1, n01=0) produces a two‑sided exact p of 1.00 under the standard calculation used for small discordant counts; informally, with only a single discordant pair the test cannot exclude the symmetric chance that the single discordance is random under the null. The bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) bounds plausible absolute improvement under the run's sampling semantics. The preregistered planning target (≈+0.30 absolute) is orders of magnitude larger than the empirically resolvable improvement in this run; the observed near‑ceiling baseline therefore invalidates the preregistered power assumption.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the single observed invalid baseline output, demonstrating that the implemented deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration can remediate at least some validator‑detected violations. However, the run provides no evidence that the guarded pipeline yields the large preregistered effect (≥50% relative reduction in fail rate) because the baseline pass rate was far higher than planned. Operationally, two distinct lessons arise.

First, task‑bank difficulty calibration matters. Confirmatory designs that target substantial absolute improvements must ensure the baseline failure rate leaves statistical headroom. Our preregistered planning assumed baseline pass rate = 0.40; an empirical baseline near 1.0 eliminates detectability for large preregistered effects. For practical NetOps readiness claims, experimenters should either (a) design or adversarially augment task banks to produce meaningful baseline failure prevalence, or (b) adopt alternative estimands focused on repair efficacy conditional on initial failure rather than absolute population‑level risk reduction.

Second, paired semantics and repair budgets are inferentially consequential. Reusing a shared initial candidate per pair reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference; independent draws increase discordant‑pair potential but introduce cross‑arm heterogeneity. The choice must be prespecified and power‑checked. Similarly, restricting repair to a single automated iteration bounds operational realism; production guardrails often permit multiple automated repair attempts plus human approval. Future confirmatory studies should preregister realistic repair budgets and sample sizes that target a planned number of initial failures to precisely estimate repair success.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the shared_initial_candidate pairing choice (increasing within‑pair correlation). Construct validity is limited because deterministic validator checks do not execute configurations in a live network; we did not measure runtime effects (packet‑level reachability or performance) and instead used canonicalized configuration and constraint checks as the operational proxy. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, constrained vendor‑template scope, single model family (gpt-5-mini), and the single validator implementation. Conclusion validity is constrained by the small number of informative discordant pairs; statistical inference about large preregistered effects is therefore not supported by the observed data.

Reproducibility and archival practice: All raw model outputs, per‑task validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts were archived with the run. Key archival artifacts include the execution manifest and the analysis artifact bundle (condition_summary.csv, paired_contingency_table.csv, paired_bootstrap results, and analysis logs). These artifacts contain the exact per‑task normalized responses, validator decisions, and repair traces used to compute the tabulated counts and intervals reported here. Interested readers can consult the archived execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement for per‑task diagnostics and to reproduce the reported analyses. We intentionally avoid embedding low‑level run file paths in the prose; artifact names and the manifest provide machine‑verifiable provenance.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations: calibrate task difficulty to produce sufficient initial failures, preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets, and measure runtime semantic effects (emulation or simulation) where operational claims are required. Full archived artifacts accompany this manuscript to support reproducibility and method refinement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor-template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.

Sampling semantics (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
